Control

Temperature-limited heating pulses

Download Markdown ↓

Rev08 · Single-channel model and implementation

Summary

  • End each fixed-amplitude heating pulse at an estimated temperature ceiling or its requested duration. This controls pulse termination; tactile displacement and force remain separate quantities to measure.
  • Predict two temperatures: metal and surrounding material. Electrical power heats the metal, while the surroundings retain heat between pulses. Three fitted heat-transfer coefficients describe this exchange.
  • Correct the predicted metal temperature using measured resistance and the calibrated resistance–temperature curve. The model carries the heating and cooling history; resistance supplies a new observation. A short table search balances their agreement.
  • Check nonmonotonicity explicitly. Search near the predicted temperature and stop when two distinct resistance-compatible branches remain. Where resistance changes little with temperature, the model supplies most of the estimate.
  • Use a measured stopping allowance and a local timer. The allowance covers observed underestimation; the timer accounts for further heating and switch delay. Fit on one experiment and check fixed settings on another. The result is an effective-temperature estimate with experimentally established operating scope.

1. One heater and its inputs

One electrical measurement and the stored thermal state supply each control cycle.

Single-channel heating, measurement and temperature controlEnlarge figure ↗

The adjustable supply powers one resistive heater through a switch. Separate voltage-sense connections measure across the active metal; current measurement includes any sensing-network current that bypasses the current sensor. The controller receives corrected, time-aligned voltage V\mathsf{V}V and current I\mathsf{I}I.

UPDATE(t, T, S, average_power, V, I, settled_reading, heating)
    returns updated T, S, measurement_status and switch_off_deadline

A measured material curve can serve pixels made from the same stock; each pixel needs its own R0\mathsf{R_0}R0​.

2. Predict heating and retained heat

The thermal model predicts the next temperatures before the resistance reading is used.

Use

C(T)dTdt=P−G(T−S),dSdt=β(T−S)−γ(S−A).\mathsf{C(T)\frac{dT}{dt}=P-G(T-S),\qquad \frac{dS}{dt}=\beta(T-S)-\gamma(S-A).}C(T)dtdT​=P−G(T−S),dtdS​=β(T−S)−γ(S−A).

Electrical power heats the metal. The term G(T−S)\mathsf{G(T-S)}G(T−S) transfers heat between metal and surroundings. The second equation represents warming and cooling of the effective surrounding material. Its temperature S\mathsf{S}S persists during pauses, so two otherwise identical pulses can begin from different thermal conditions.

For a short interval, the prediction is

Tpred=T+ΔtP−G(T−S)C(T),Spred=S+Δt[β(T−S)−γ(S−A)].\mathsf{T_{\rm pred}=T+\Delta t\frac{P-G(T-S)}{C(T)},\qquad S_{\rm pred}=S+\Delta t[\beta(T-S)-\gamma(S-A)].}Tpred​=T+ΔtC(T)P−G(T−S)​,Spred​=S+Δt[β(T−S)−γ(S−A)].

Use the old T,S\mathsf{T,S}T,S on both right-hand sides. Divide longer intervals into steps no greater than one tenth of the smaller time scale Cmin⁡/G\mathsf{C_{\min}/G}Cmin​/G and 1/(β+γ)\mathsf{1/(\beta+\gamma)}1/(β+γ), where Cmin⁡\mathsf{C_{\min}}Cmin​ is the minimum heat capacity over the operating range. This is a practical integration setting; halve it during the offline replay and check that the change is small compared with the selected temperature resolution.

Calculate the power input in the same way during fitting and operation:

  1. Settled heating: average two consecutive measured powers from the same continuous ON interval, P=(VoldIold+VI)/2\mathsf{P=(V_{\rm old}I_{\rm old}+VI)/2}P=(Vold​Iold​+VI)/2.
  2. Switching and analog settling: use P=Pmax⁡\mathsf{P=P_{\max}}P=Pmax​ during the measured settling interval. Calculate Pmax⁡=Vmax⁡2/Rmin⁡\mathsf{P_{\max}=V_{\max}^2/R_{\min}}Pmax​=Vmax2​/Rmin​, with the largest checked terminal voltage, including excursions, and the smallest calibrated metal resistance.
  3. OFF time: use the measured residual power.
  4. Split an update at each switch transition or settling boundary; apply the corresponding power to each part.

Initialize T=S=A\mathsf{T=S=A}T=S=A after the measured cooling period. Continue updating both temperatures during every pause.

3. Convert the resistance curve into a correction

The calibrated curve relates candidate temperatures to resistance; the update compares those predictions with the measured resistance.

For a stock curve measured at a different ambient, first normalize it at the operating ambient: q(T)=qcal(T)/qcal(A)\mathsf{q(T)=q_{\rm cal}(T)/q_{\rm cal}(A)}q(T)=qcal​(T)/qcal​(A). Then q(A)=1\mathsf{q(A)=1}q(A)=1 matches the current pixel's measured R0\mathsf{R_0}R0​. Recalculate the normalized error allowance with this scaling and ambient/reference-resistance uncertainty. Store the resulting pairs (Tj,qj)\mathsf{(T_j,q_j)}(Tj​,qj​), ordered by temperature. Between adjacent points, use

q(U)=qj+qj+1−qjTj+1−Tj(U−Tj),\mathsf{q(U)=q_j+\frac{q_{j+1}-q_j}{T_{j+1}-T_j}(U-T_j),}q(U)=qj​+Tj+1​−Tj​qj+1​−qj​​(U−Tj​),

where U\mathsf{U}U is a candidate temperature. Include points around each observed turning region. Interpolation represents the measured curve; its remaining error belongs in eR\mathsf{e_R}eR​.

During settled conduction calculate

y=VIR0.\mathsf{y=\frac{V}{I R_0}.}y=IR0​V​.

Prepare a table of q(U)\mathsf{q(U)}q(U) at 1 °C spacing, using the interpolation above. Also calculate L\mathsf{L}L, the largest absolute interpolation slope. For each table temperature within Tpred±w\mathsf{T_{\rm pred}\pm w}Tpred​±w, test

∣y−q(U)∣≤e,e=eR+L (1 ∘C).\mathsf{|y-q(U)|\le e,\qquad e=e_R+L\,(1\ ^\circ\mathrm C).}∣y−q(U)∣≤e,e=eR​+L(1 ∘C).

The second term allows for the grid and a window boundary between grid points. The 1 °C spacing is a numerical resolution, not a measurement accuracy. Require w≥1\mathsf{w\ge1}w≥1 K. Consecutive passing grid indices form a continuous run. No run means disagreement between the electrical reading and the allowed correction. More than one separated run means that distinct local resistance branches remain. Either result ends the heating pulse.

When one run remains, choose its temperature minimizing

J(U)=(U−Tpredw)2+(y−q(U)eR)2.\mathsf{J(U)=\left(\frac{U-T_{\rm pred}}{w}\right)^2+ \left(\frac{y-q(U)}{e_R}\right)^2.}J(U)=(wU−Tpred​​)2+(eR​y−q(U)​)2.

Also evaluate J\mathsf{J}J at the continuous prediction Tpred\mathsf{T_{\rm pred}}Tpred​ itself, using interpolated resistance, if it passes the same resistance test. Select the lower-cost candidate; choose the continuous prediction on a tie. This preserves temperature changes smaller than a grid step. Set T\mathsf{T}T to the selected temperature and S=Spred\mathsf{S=S_{\rm pred}}S=Spred​. The calculation balances the prediction against resistance agreement. A flat q\mathsf{q}q gives nearly equal resistance scores; the first term then keeps the estimate near the prediction. A steep slope makes resistance more informative. The initialized thermal history selects the search region; resistance distinguishes temperatures within it.

Set two fixed correction settings:

  1. Resistance allowance eR\mathsf{e_R}eR​: add the checked electrical-error allowance and the curve-error allowance, both expressed as fractions of R0\mathsf{R_0}R0​. Include reference uncertainty, observed heating–cooling variation and the stated interpolation allowance. Store a positive value.
  2. Search width w\mathsf{w}w: compare the uncorrected model with aligned independent temperature readings on the fitting experiment. Take the largest absolute temperature difference, add reference uncertainty and 1 K, and use at least 1 K. Keep this width fixed for validation.

When independent temperature readings are unavailable, w\mathsf{w}w is a declared engineering setting. Section 5 states the operating claim supported by that case.

Illustrative curve. Suppose measured anchors were (20,1.000),(400,1.040),(600,1.060),(800,1.040)\mathsf{(20,1.000),(400,1.040),(600,1.060),(800,1.040)}(20,1.000),(400,1.040),(600,1.060),(800,1.040). These values illustrate the calculation and are not a NiCr calibration. A reading y=1.050\mathsf{y=1.050}y=1.050 has solutions near 500 and 700 °C. With Tpred=510\mathsf{T_{\rm pred}=510}Tpred​=510 °C and w=20\mathsf{w=20}w=20 K, only the neighborhood of 500 °C is searched. With a prediction of 600 °C and a 120 K search window, both branches remain and heating stops.

4. End a heating pulse

Each pulse ends at the earliest temperature, duration or data-age limit.

The requested pulse specifies fixed voltage, maximum duration and Tc\mathsf{T_c}Tc​. Set the stopping allowance M\mathsf{M}M from the completed observer on the fitting experiment:

  1. At each aligned reference reading, subtract the corrected estimate from the independently measured temperature.
  2. Keep the largest positive difference, or zero if all differences are negative.
  3. Add the temperature-reference uncertainty and 1 K for the numerical grid.
  4. Check this fixed allowance on the separate validation experiment.

At state time t\mathsf{t}t, calculate

ttemperature=t+[Tc−M−max⁡(T,S)]Cmin⁡Pmax⁡−τoff,\mathsf{t_{\rm temperature}=t+ \frac{[T_c-M-\max(T,S)]C_{\min}}{P_{\max}}-\tau_{\rm off},}ttemperature​=t+Pmax​[Tc​−M−max(T,S)]Cmin​​−τoff​,

where Pmax⁡\mathsf{P_{\max}}Pmax​ bounds delivered heater power, including switching excursions, and τoff\mathsf{\tau_{\rm off}}τoff​ is the measured timer/physical-turn-off delay. Set the local timer to the earliest of this deadline, the original requested pulse end, and the last valid reading plus the permitted data age minus τoff\mathsf{\tau_{\rm off}}τoff​. Turn off immediately if that time has passed.

The hotter model state cannot increase through passive internal heat exchange alone. Added electrical power gives the rise allowance Pmax⁡/Cmin⁡\mathsf{P_{\max}/C_{\min}}Pmax​/Cmin​. The stopping rule combines this modeled rise with the experimentally checked allowance M\mathsf{M}M.

One clock cycle. Take illustrative values T=500\mathsf{T=500}T=500, S=100\mathsf{S=100}S=100, A=20\mathsf{A=20}A=20 °C; C=0.001\mathsf{C=0.001}C=0.001 J/K, G=0.001\mathsf{G=0.001}G=0.001 W/K, β=1\mathsf{\beta=1}β=1, γ=0.2\mathsf{\gamma=0.2}γ=0.2 s⁻¹; P=10.4\mathsf{P=10.4}P=10.4 W and Δt=0.001\mathsf{\Delta t=0.001}Δt=0.001 s. The prediction is Tpred=510\mathsf{T_{\rm pred}=510}Tpred​=510, Spred=100.384\mathsf{S_{\rm pred}=100.384}Spred​=100.384 °C. With the illustrative curve, y=1.050\mathsf{y=1.050}y=1.050, w=20\mathsf{w=20}w=20 K and eR=0.001\mathsf{e_R=0.001}eR​=0.001, the grid minimum is 502 °C: its prediction and resistance contributions to J\mathsf{J}J are 0.16 and 0.04.

For Tc=550\mathsf{T_c=550}Tc​=550 °C, M=15\mathsf{M=15}M=15 K, Pmax⁡=12\mathsf{P_{\max}=12}Pmax​=12 W, Cmin⁡=0.001\mathsf{C_{\min}=0.001}Cmin​=0.001 J/K and τoff=50\mathsf{\tau_{\rm off}=50}τoff​=50 µs, the temperature deadline is 2.70 ms after this state time. A shorter requested duration or earlier data expiry takes precedence.

5. Fit once, then validate separately

Parameter fitting and validation use different recorded sequences.

The fitting experiment identifies G,β,γ\mathsf{G,\beta,\gamma}G,β,γ. Choose a checked pulse width tp\mathsf{t_p}tp​ and onset interval tr>tp\mathsf{t_r>t_p}tr​>tp​; keep the voltage fixed. Log gate transitions, voltage, current and ambient temperature throughout:

  1. From ambient, apply one pulse of width tp\mathsf{t_p}tp​; wait 4tr\mathsf{4t_r}4tr​ after turn-off.
  2. Apply four pulses, with starts separated by tr\mathsf{t_r}tr​.
  3. Wait tr\mathsf{t_r}tr​ after the last turn-off; apply one pulse.
  4. Wait 4tr\mathsf{4t_r}4tr​ after turn-off; apply one final pulse.

The isolated pulse identifies rapid heating. The train and restart pulses reveal heat retained between pulses.

For each positive candidate G,β,γ\mathsf{G,\beta,\gamma}G,β,γ, replay the complete record from ambient using the power-input recipe and prediction equations. Do not apply resistance corrections during this replay. Minimize

Jfit=∑k∈settled readings[q(T(tk))−Vk/(IkR0)eR]2.\mathsf{J_{\rm fit}=\sum_{k\in\text{settled readings}} \left[\frac{q(T(t_k))-V_k/(I_kR_0)}{e_R}\right]^2.}Jfit​=k∈settled readings∑​[eR​q(T(tk​))−Vk​/(Ik​R0​)​]2.

Fix heat capacity from the measured geometry and material data. Three fitted coefficients then describe heat transfer. Appendix B gives a small derivative-free search. Independent temperature observations, where available, distinguish fits with similar resistance predictions but different temperature histories.

For foil, a pyrometer can provide these observations when its spot lies on the active metal, emissivity is calibrated, and its temporal response resolves the experiment. Begin with sufficiently slow pulses for that instrument. For ultrafine wire, the same-stock equilibrium calibration establishes the material curve; it does not supply in-pulse temperature observations.

The validation experiment checks the completed controller with fixed coefficients, eR,w,M\mathsf{e_R,w,M}eR​,w,M, voltage and load range:

  1. From the same initial ambient condition, apply four pulses with alternating widths tp/2,tp,tp/2,tp\mathsf{t_p/2,t_p,t_p/2,t_p}tp​/2,tp​,tp​/2,tp​, starting every tr\mathsf{t_r}tr​.
  2. Wait 2tr\mathsf{2t_r}2tr​ after the final turn-off, then apply one pulse of width tp\mathsf{t_p}tp​.
  3. Use full-duration pulses throughout if a half pulse supplies no settled reading.

Evaluate four outcomes:

  1. Predicted and measured resistance agree without refitting.
  2. Independent temperature, where resolved, stays within the stated stopping allowance and below the ceiling after turn-off.
  3. The observer remains on a coherent branch and permits useful displacement or force.
  4. Pulse termination and retained heating behave correctly under the intended mechanical load.

Agreement in resistance tests electrical prediction, including across a nonmonotonic curve. Without resolved independent temperature data, use the observer as experimental estimate-based pulse control within the previously checked finite-pulse protocol; M\mathsf{M}M remains a declared engineering margin. A demonstrated temperature-error allowance requires the independent reference. Restrict operation to the checked pulse, load and repetition range.

Appendix A. Clock-cycle arithmetic

The following calculation runs once per channel update.

The table contains candidate temperature U and interpolated q. A settled reading is invalid if it times out, saturates, or has current below the calibrated measurement range. permitted_data_age is the configured maximum delay between valid readings. Time t is the update endpoint; state_time is the previously represented time. Split intervals at switching events. The electrical routine supplies interval-average P and a valid settled reading flag.

UPDATE(t, T, S, P, V, I, settled, heating):
    if t <= state_time: switch OFF; return timestamp_fault
    if heating and settled and readings_invalid: switch OFF; return measurement_fault
    remaining = t-state_time
    hmax = 0.1*min(Cmin/G, 1/(beta+gamma))
    while remaining > 0:
        h = min(remaining,hmax)
        Tnew = T + h*(P-G*(T-S))/C(T)
        Snew = S + h*(beta*(T-S)-gamma*(S-A))
        T = Tnew; S = Snew; remaining = remaining-h; state_time = state_time+h
        if T is outside calibration: switch OFF; return range_fault
    state_time = t
    if not heating: return T, S
    if settled:
        y = V/(I*R0)
        predicted = T; best_cost = infinity; runs = 0; previous_pass = false
        for consecutive grid entries with abs(U-predicted) <= w:
            passes = abs(y-q) <= eR + L*grid_step
            if passes and not previous_pass: runs = runs+1
            if passes:
                cost = ((U-predicted)/w)^2 + ((y-q)/eR)^2
                if cost < best_cost: best_cost = cost; best_T = U
            previous_pass = passes
        if runs != 1: switch OFF; return mismatch_or_ambiguity
        q_pred = interpolate_q(predicted)
        if abs(y-q_pred) <= eR + L*grid_step:
            cost = ((y-q_pred)/eR)^2
            if cost <= best_cost: best_T = predicted
        T = best_T; last_valid_time = t
    temperature_end = t + (Tc-M-max(T,S))*Cmin/Pmax - turn_off_delay
    data_end = last_valid_time + permitted_data_age - turn_off_delay
    deadline = min(original_pulse_end,temperature_end,data_end)
    if deadline <= now: switch OFF
    else: arm local switch-off timer for deadline
    return T, S, deadline

A fault preserves the last computed state and disables subsequent pulses. Before starting a pulse, update OFF cooling to its start time, set last_valid_time to that time, and fix original_pulse_end = start_time + requested_duration. Calculate the same deadline above. In one short uninterrupted operation, check that the deadline is future, arm the timer and enable the switch; otherwise leave it OFF. Record the actual gate transition. The data-expiry term supplies the first-reading deadline. After reset, complete the established cooldown before initializing to ambient.

Appendix B. Reproducible coefficient search

A direct multiplicative search gives a reproducible initial fit.

Use reference values G=C(A)/tp\mathsf{G=C(A)/t_p}G=C(A)/tp​, β=1/tr\mathsf{\beta=1/t_r}β=1/tr​, γ=1/(4tr)\mathsf{\gamma=1/(4t_r)}γ=1/(4tr​). Try exactly three starts, multiplying all three reference values together by 0.1, 1 or 10. This is a small local search; independent temperature checks distinguish physically different fits.

COST(G, beta, gamma):
    set T=A, S=A, cost=0
    replay every logged power interval using the prediction equations
    at each valid resistance sample:
        cost = cost + ((q(T)-V/(I*R0))/eR)^2
    return cost, or infinity if temperature leaves calibration

FIT():
    for common starting factor 0.1, 1 and 10:
        coefficients = starting_factor * reference_coefficients
        ratio = 2
        for at most 200 search rounds:
            evaluate current coefficients and six alternatives:
                multiply or divide one coefficient by ratio
            if an alternative lowers COST: retain the best alternative
            else: ratio = sqrt(ratio)
            if ratio < 1.02: finish this start
        if search completed and cost is finite: retain fit and predicted temperatures
    if no finite completed fit remains: return fitting_failure
    return the lowest-cost completed fit and the other completed fits

Inspect systematic residuals and alternative temperature histories. Unfinished searches or incompatible independent temperatures require resolving that specific fit before operation. The validation record remains separate from fitting and allowance selection.

Appendix C. Physical interpretation and processor implementation

The processor executes the same arithmetic as the offline replay.

A Teensy 4.1 can perform the single-channel arithmetic locally. The macro circuit measures current and both terminal voltages; the wire channel measures shunt current and selected differential voltage. Apply each circuit's measured bypass-current correction before forming VI\mathsf{VI}VI or V/I\mathsf{V/I}V/I. USB transfers configuration and buffered records outside the pulse-control calculation.

The model has consistent physical units: power divided by heat capacity has units K/s; G(T−S)\mathsf{G(T-S)}G(T−S) has units W; the two heat-transfer rates have units s⁻¹; all three fitted coefficients are positive. The passive model cools toward ambient with power removed. The inferred T\mathsf{T}T is a resistance-related effective metal temperature, distinct from the spatial peak at a hotspot. The two-state description and finite correction window must explain the intended pulse history before their estimates are used to end pulses.
